keySentence: Peter Pan never wanted to grow up — he chose wonder over responsibility.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Most children dream about the day they will finally be old enough to make their own decisions. But Peter Pan looked at the adult world and saw nothing that he wanted or needed for himself. Adults had forgotten how to fly and how to play and how to believe in things that seemed impossible. They were too tired and too serious to notice the magic that was still all around them every day. Peter chose to remain in Neverland where every morning brought a completely new adventure waiting. He knew what his choice cost him and he made it anyway with his eyes completely open and clear. Peter Pan never wanted to grow up — he chose wonder over responsibility.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Every child eventually reaches the moment when the adult world begins to seem more real than Neverland. But Peter Pan reached that moment and turned away from it with a firm and completely deliberate step. He had seen what responsibility looked like — the tired eyes, the unpaid bills, the forgotten songs. He had seen what happened to the people who stopped believing in things they could not immediately explain. Neverland was not simply a place of fun and games for Peter — it was a serious alternative to forgetting. He believed that a life without wonder was not a grown-up life at all but simply a diminished one. His choice had real costs, as all genuine choices do, and Peter accepted every one of them willingly. Peter Pan never wanted to grow up — he chose wonder over responsibility.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: J.M. Barrie presents Peter Pan's choice not as childish escapism but as a genuine moral position. Peter has evaluated the terms of adulthood with more care than most adults ever apply to the same question. He knows what he is giving up — connection, continuity, the particular love of people who watch you grow. And he knows what he is keeping — wonder, freedom, the perpetual freshness of a world that never becomes routine. What makes Peter both admirable and heartbreaking is the completeness of his self-knowledge on this point. He is not confused about what growing up means — he simply values different things than most people do. The story asks us to consider whether the adult world has perhaps forgotten to ask the question Peter asked. We grow up because everyone does, not always because we have carefully chosen what we are choosing to become. Peter Pan never wanted to grow up — he chose wonder over responsibility.
